---
name: sls-3-reading
description: SLS step 3. Read the newly included papers (or one, by P ID), draft their records, check their citations, and accept them.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: "[P{n}]"
---
# SLS 3 — Reading

Runs rows 3a–3c of `ai/flow-sls.md`, following `ai/running.md`.

## Work set
Every P ID included in an `sls/2-search/R*.md` file with no `sls/3-reading/P{n}.md` yet. With an argument, only that paper.

## Rows
0. **PDFs** — run `just papers-pull`, so PDFs published from another machine are in `research/papers/`.
1. **3a** — dispatch one `reader` per paper, in parallel. Inputs: the paper (`papers/P{n}.pdf` if present, and its reference line from the round file), `sls/1-protocol/quality.md`, `extraction-form.md`, `criteria.md`, and the accepted `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md` once any exist. For a paper whose round-file reason says "full text decides": read the abstract and introduction first and stop early, recording the X criterion, when one clearly applies. Outputs: `sls/3-reading/P{n}.md`, and `papers/P{n}.pdf` if the reader downloads it.
2. **3b** — dispatch one `citation-checker` per record, in parallel. Inputs: `P{n}.md`, the paper. Output: `P{n}.citations.md`.
3. **3c** — gate, one decision per record. At this gate, tell me which papers my argument depends on: I read those in full before deciding.

4. **Publish** — run `just papers-push`, so every PDF in `research/papers/` is published to the `papers` release of the GitHub repo.

Done when every paper in the work set has a decided record and its PDF, if any, is published.
# Flow: SLS

Rows run by the `sls` skill (`skills.md`), after step 0 (`kickstart.md`). Paths are relative to `research/`. `{n}` is an ID number, `{k}` a round number. Every gate also writes one decision file (`ai-log.md`). `↺` rows are loop decisions.

| # | Who | Input | Output | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SLS 1 Protocol** · `sls-1-protocol` | | | | |
| 1a | `protocol-critic` | `0-start/*.md` | `sls/1-protocol/`: `need.md`, `SQ{n}.md`, `criteria.md`, `quality.md`, `extraction-form.md` | — |
| 1b | `skeptic` | `0-start/*.md`, `sls/1-protocol/SQ*.md` | `sls/1-protocol/SQ{n}.md` (counter-evidence SQs), `protocol.skeptic.md` | — |
| 1c | Me | 1a + 1b files | Status of each set | **Protocol frozen.** Later changes: `sls/1-protocol/changes/{date}-{slug}.md` |
| **SLS 2 Search** · `sls-2-search` | | | | |
| 2a | `snowballer` | `sls/1-protocol/criteria.md`, `0-start/seeds.md` | `sls/2-search/search-string.md`, `R0.md` (candidates, each with its I/X criterion) | — |
| 2b | Me | `sls/2-search/R0.md` | P IDs assigned in `R0.md` | **Include/exclude** |
| 2c | `snowballer` | `sls/2-search/R{k-1}*.md`, `sls/1-protocol/criteria.md` | `sls/2-search/R{k}-backward.md`, `R{k}-forward.md` | — |
| 2d | Me | 2c files | P IDs assigned | **Include/exclude** |
| **SLS 3 Reading** · `sls-3-reading` (for each new P) | | | | |
| 3a | `reader` | `papers/P{n}.pdf` (else the paper online), `sls/1-protocol/quality.md`, `extraction-form.md`, `SQ*.md`, accepted `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md` once any exist | `sls/3-reading/P{n}.md`, `papers/P{n}.pdf` if downloaded | — |
| 3b | `citation-checker` | `sls/3-reading/P{n}.md`, the paper | `sls/3-reading/P{n}.citations.md` | — |
| 3c | Me | 3a + 3b files | Status set; key papers proposed (`sls/3-reading/step.md`); PDFs published with `just papers-push` | **Record accepted** |
| **SLS 4 Synthesis** · `sls-4-synthesis` | | | | |
| 4a | `synthesizer` | Accepted `sls/3-reading/P*.md`, `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md` | `sls/4-synthesis/C{n}.md` (definition, papers, comparison), new or updated | — |
| 4b | Me | 4a files | Status set; merges and splits; key papers updated | **Concepts accepted** |
| ↺ | `just check` | Last `sls/2-search/R{k}*.md` | New papers? Yes → 2c. No → 5a | Stop rule [1] |
| **SLS 5 Gap** · `sls-5-gap` | | | | |
| 5a | `synthesizer` | Accepted `sls/4-synthesis/C*.md`, `sls/1-protocol/SQ*.md` | `sls/5-gap/`: `SQ{n}.answer.md`, `gap.md`, `solutions.md`, `history.md`, `limitations.md` | — |
| 5b | `skeptic` | 5a files | `sls/5-gap/gap.skeptic.md` | — |
| 5c | Me | 5a + 5b files | Status set; key papers extended from `gap.md` and read in full | **Gap** |

Next: row 6a (`flow-dsrm.md`).

---

## References
1. Wohlin (2014). *Guidelines for Snowballing in Systematic Literature Studies*. Conference on Evaluation and Assessment in Software Engineering.
# Step 3 — Reading and extraction

> **Inputs:** a paper included in `2-search/`, `1-protocol/quality.md`, `1-protocol/extraction-form.md` · **Next:** `4-synthesis/`

> Keshav [1]: read in up to three passes, stopping when the paper has given what you need.
> Kitchenham and Charters [2]: assess quality and extract the same fields from every paper.

## Rules
- Every extracted value and concept has a page.
- Papers my argument depends on (key papers) are read in full by me. A paper is key if it passes at least one test:
  1. **Sole or main evidence:** it is the only paper, or one of very few, answering an SQ.
  2. **Load-bearing claim:** the problem or the gap rests on a claim it makes.
  3. **Strongest counter-evidence:** it argues most strongly against the observation.
  4. **Seed:** it is in `0-start/seeds.md`.
- Key papers are proposed, with the test each passes, at 3c (provisional); updated at each 4b from the papers each accepted concept rests on; extended at 5c with any paper `5-gap/gap.md` rests on; and read in full before the gap gate (5c) is decided. Change: `1-protocol/changes/2026-10-12-key-papers.md`.

## Produces
Template in `ai/template/sls/3-reading/`. Flow rows 3a–3c (`ai/flow-sls.md`).

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `P{n}.md` | The record of one paper: five Cs, quality, extracted fields, concepts |
| `P{n}.citations.md` | The citation check of that record |

---

## References
1. Keshav (2007). *How to Read a Paper*. Association for Computing Machinery Special Interest Group on Data Communication, Computer Communication Review 37(3).
2. Kitchenham, Charters (2007). *Guidelines for Performing Systematic Literature Reviews in Software Engineering*. Keele University and Durham University technical report.

## Rules
- Every extracted value and concept has a page.
- Papers my argument depends on (key papers) are read in full by me. A paper is key if it passes at least one test:
  1. **Sole or main evidence:** it is the only paper, or one of very few, answering an SQ.
  2. **Load-bearing claim:** the problem or the gap rests on a claim it makes.
  3. **Strongest counter-evidence:** it argues most strongly against the observation.
  4. **Seed:** it is in `0-start/seeds.md`.
- Key papers are proposed, with the test each passes, at 3c (provisional); updated at each 4b from the papers each accepted concept rests on; extended at 5c with any paper `5-gap/gap.md` rests on; and read in full before the gap gate (5c) is decided. ---
id: change-2026-10-12-key-papers
row: 1c
by: me
status: accepted
inputs: [sls/3-reading/step.md]
---
# Protocol change: key-papers

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-12-key-papers.md`.

## What changed
- `sls/3-reading/step.md`, *Rules*:
  - Before: "Papers my argument depends on are read in full by me." No test said which papers those are, and the 3c skill asked for them to be read before each 3c decision.
  - After: a paper is key if it passes at least one of four tests (sole or main evidence for an SQ; a claim the problem or gap rests on; strongest counter-evidence; a seed in `0-start/seeds.md`). Key papers are proposed at 3c (provisional), updated at each 4b from the papers each accepted concept rests on, extended at 5c with any paper `5-gap/gap.md` rests on, and read in full by me before the gap gate (5c) is decided.
- Outside the protocol, to match: `ai/flow-sls.md` rows 3c, 4b and 5c; the `sls-3-reading`, `sls-4-synthesis` and `sls-5-gap` skills.

## Why
Which papers I read in full was decided case by case, from the assistant's proposal, with no stated rule. At 3c the argument does not exist yet: it is built at synthesis (4a) and the gap (5a), so which papers it rests on can only be known from the concept files and `gap.md`.

## Papers affected
None re-screened or re-read. P8, P9, P10 and P12 no longer wait at 3c for my full reading; they are read before 5c if they are key.
---
id: change-2026-10-06-reading-pilot
row: 1c
by: me
status: accepted
inputs: [sls/1-protocol/extraction-form.md, sls/1-protocol/quality.md, sls/1-protocol/criteria.md]
---
# Protocol change: reading-pilot

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md`.

## What changed
- `extraction-form.md`:
  - New *Applies to* column (I1–I4 per field); a field outside the paper's criteria is `n/a (I3)`, and `not stated` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
  - Values in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* are tagged measured / simulated / design figure / analytical / read off.
  - *Reference*: pages are those printed on `papers/P*.pdf` (else its PDF page), with the version (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), the publisher's page range and any offset; abstract-only content cites `abstract`. Criteria I1–I4.
  - *Paper type*: one or more types, plus "position or analytical argument".
  - *Levels with message semantics*: adds `partly` (a message is a primitive at the level but other paths exist, naming the message-only operations), and for kernels and multicomputers separate answers between cores or nodes and within a core.
- `quality.md`:
  - Scale adds `n/a`, only for a source not read or a question that cannot apply, with the reason.

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.
- Each decision that is mine as a choice: two to four concrete options, the exact edit each one makes to which file, and the one you recommend. The gate asks me with these (`ai/gate.md`).
# Gate

How a skill runs a gate row. The decision is mine; the skill prepares it, records it, and checks it.

1. **Present.** For each file waiting at this gate: its path, one line on what it holds, and every flag raised by its reviews (`.skeptic.md`, `.citations.md`, `.examiner.md` next to it). Give the paths so I can open the files myself. Show a file's content when I ask; never make me judge from a bare list.
2. **Ask** with the AskUserQuestion tool, not in prose, so every decision is a choice:
   - **Order.** Files that others depend on first (e.g. SQs before `criteria.md` and `extraction-form.md`, which must serve the kept SQs). Open decisions the agents named as mine come before the files they affect.
   - **One question per file**, up to four per call. Options: *Accept*; one option per concrete fix a review or the agent suggested, with the exact edit in its description (*multiSelect* when the fixes are independent); *Reject*. *Other* takes my own edits.
   - **Unflagged files** may be offered together in one *multiSelect* question ("accept these"); any I leave unselected get their own question.
   - **Recommend** one option when the reviews support it, marked "(Recommended)" and listed first.
3. **Wait** for my decision on each file: accept, change, or reject. My decision is the only input to the next step; a file I have not decided on stays `proposed`.
4. **Apply.**
   - Accept: `status: accepted`.
   - Change: apply exactly the edits I give, then `status: changed`.
   - Reject: `status: rejected`.
   - Gates that assign values in a table (P IDs in 2b and 2d) write those values too.
5. **Record.** One decision file per decided file, from `ai/template/ai-log/decision.md`, saved as `research/ai-log/decisions/{date}-{row}-{id}.md`. *What I changed and why* holds my words. *Raw log entries* holds the session ID given at session start and the time span from the row's first dispatch to this gate (`ai/ai-log.md`).
6. **Check.** Run `just check`.

The gate is done when every file waiting at it has a status other than `proposed` and a decision file.

# Thesis task runner

# Default recipe (runs if you just type 'just')
default: help

# Display help
help:
    @just --list

# Build thesis PDF
build:
    latexmk -pdf thesis.tex

# Live preview (recompile on save)
preview:
    latexmk -pvc -pdf thesis.tex

# Clean auxiliary files
clean:
    latexmk -c
    rm -f thesis.pdf

# Regenerate all diagrams
diagrams:
    dot -Tpng design/ontology/ontology.dot -o design/ontology/ontology.png
    echo "✓ Ontology diagram"
    @if [ -f design/language/sequence.mmd ]; then \
        mmdc -i design/language/sequence.mmd -o design/language/sequence.png; \
        echo "✓ Sequence diagram"; \
    fi

# Search in thesis
search term:
    rg "{{ term }}" chapters/ research/ --type tex --type md

# Count words
wordcount:
    @echo "Total words:"
    @wc -w chapters/*.tex | tail -1

   - **Unflagged files** may be offered together in one *multiSelect* question ("accept these"); any I leave unselected get their own question.
   - **Recommend** one option when the reviews support it, marked "(Recommended)" and listed first.
3. **Wait** for my decision on each file: accept, change, or reject. My decision is the only input to the next step; a file I have not decided on stays `proposed`.
4. **Apply.**
   - Accept: `status: accepted`.
   - Change: apply exactly the edits I give, then `status: changed`.
   - Reject: `status: rejected`.
   - Gates that assign values in a table (P IDs in 2b and 2d) write those values too.
5. **Record.** One decision file per decided file, from `ai/template/ai-log/decision.md`, saved as `research/ai-log/decisions/{date}-{row}-{id}.md`. *What I changed and why* holds my words. *Raw log entries* holds the session ID given at session start and the time span from the row's first dispatch to this gate (`ai/ai-log.md`).
6. **Check.** Run `just check`.

The gate is done when every file waiting at it has a status other than `proposed` and a decision file.

# Thesis task runner

# Default recipe (runs if you just type 'just')
default: help

# Display help
help:
    @just --list

# Build thesis PDF
build:
    latexmk -pdf thesis.tex

# Live preview (recompile on save)
preview:
    latexmk -pvc -pdf thesis.tex

# Clean auxiliary files
clean:
    latexmk -c
    rm -f thesis.pdf

# Regenerate all diagrams
diagrams:
    dot -Tpng design/ontology/ontology.dot -o design/ontology/ontology.png
    echo "✓ Ontology diagram"
    @if [ -f design/language/sequence.mmd ]; then \
        mmdc -i design/language/sequence.mmd -o design/language/sequence.png; \
        echo "✓ Sequence diagram"; \
    fi

# Search in thesis
search term:
    rg "{{ term }}" chapters/ research/ --type tex --type md

# Count words
wordcount:
    @echo "Total words:"
    @wc -w chapters/*.tex | tail -1

Steele and Gabriel 1993, *The Evolution of Lisp* (P15), is back: 10 of 11. Its reader proposes adding I4 ("directly answers one of the later questions") through two questions, both answered only partly and in prose:
- **Does raising the hardware toward the language cost performance or generality (SQ9)?** The authors say the belief that Lisp on stock hardware could never perform well was "proven wrong", and that Le Lisp on a VAX ran about as fast as a Symbolics 3600 (pp. 25, 34–35).
- **Are message passing and other system structures equivalent (SQ10)?** Sussman and Steele found that "actors and closures were the same concept" (p. 17). Hewitt's exceptions were modifiable cells and synchronisation. This compares actors with procedure calls, not with shared memory, so it's a weaker fit for the question.

One thing to flag: the reader also added two new concept rows (p. 17 and pp. 61–62), which goes beyond the fields it was allowed to change. At the gate, you'll choose whether to keep or drop them.

I'm waiting for the last reader: Ungar 1986, *The Design and Evaluation of a High Performance Smalltalk System* (P11).

The last reader, on Ungar 1986, *The Design and Evaluation of a High Performance Smalltalk System* (P11), is back, so all 11 records are revised. It proposes adding "directly answers one of the later questions" (I4) through two questions:
- **Does raising the hardware toward the language cost performance or generality (SQ9)?** This is a clear match. The thesis argues that earlier machines "pushed the source-level semantics into the hardware, sacrificing either simplicity or performance" (p. 2).
- **What costs do independent evaluations attribute to object addressing itself, and how large are they (SQ18)?** This match is narrow. An object table would slow SOAR by 15–29% (an estimate, p. 102), but it's a software object table, and the estimate comes from the designer.

I compared every revised record with the committed version. All changes are inside the allowed fields, apart from two extras I'll put to you at the gate:
- P15 (Steele and Gabriel 1993, *The Evolution of Lisp*) gained two new concept rows.
- P49 (Tanenbaum, Herder and Bos 2006) has an earlier note relabelled.

`just check` passes.

Next, 11 citation-checkers are running in parallel. Each checks only the new or changed claims against its paper, at the cited page. When they finish, I'll open gate 3c, with one question per paper on whether to add I4.

######## P11
## Suggested fixes
The four fixes of the first check were applied at gate 3c. These are for the follow-up pass only (exact old text → new text in `P11.md`).

1. **Object-table accesses per bytecode (Attributed causes, object-table row).** `accesses the object table 12 times per bytecode [UnP83]"` → `accesses the object table 1.2 times per bytecode [UnP83]"`
2. **Static code cost (Attributed causes, object-table row).** `Static code cost of an object table: "only 2%" of the image (Table 5.14, p. 105).` → `Static code cost of an object table: it "would add only 2% to the size of the system" (p. 105; Table 5.14 gives 2.25% of a 1,500 kB image).`
3. **Compilation value is estimated (Notes, follow-up bullet).** `and the measured value of compiling to a low-level instruction set (pp. 34–35, 68)` → `and the estimated value of compiling to a low-level instruction set ("an approximate doubling in speed", p. 35; Table 4.4's 100% is a "Rough estimate based on discussion with L. P. Deutsch", p. 68)`
######## P15
## Suggested fixes
The earlier fixes (1–3: the sources sentence, "encouraged", and the Common Lisp portability goal) were applied at gate 3c. The fixes below are for claims from the follow-up pass only.

1. **Notes, follow-up bullet, the page range of section 2.8 (differs).** Section 2.8 runs to p. 19.
   - before: `with a second pass of section 2.8 (pp. 16–18)`
   - after: `with a second pass of section 2.8 (pp. 16–19)`
######## P21
## Suggested fixes

The five fixes from the first check were applied at gate 3c. Fixes for the follow-up pass only:

1. Many-core scaling, page of the programmer's view (ref. [11] title is on p. 181):
   `the programmer's view is deferred to [11] (p. 176).` → `the programmer's view is deferred to [11] (cited p. 176; "Programmer's view" in its title, p. 181).`
   and in the same row's page column:
   `| 173–174, 176–177, 179–180 |` → `| 173–174, 176–177, 179–181 |`
######## P46
## Suggested fixes

The ten fixes of the first check were applied at gate 3c and are not repeated. The fix below covers the follow-up pass only.

1. Notes, follow-up bullet, page of "the mandatory part":
   `SQ15 met: the paper argues which memory functions stay in "the mandatory part" and which go to "coexisting alternative memory servers", and what the in-kernel policy gave up (pp. 74–76).`
   →
   `SQ15 met: the paper argues which memory functions stay in the kernel, "mandatory to all other levels" (p. 76), and which go to "coexisting alternative memory servers", and what the in-kernel policy gave up (pp. 74–76).`
######## P48
## Suggested fixes
The four fixes from the first check were applied at gate 3c. The follow-up pass has no claim marked differs or not found, so there is no fix to the paper citations.

One bookkeeping point outside the citations, for the gate (no edit to a paper claim): the *Follow-up pass* bullet lists `by: reader` among the changed frontmatter fields, but the diff shows `by: reader` unchanged (only `status` and `inputs` changed). If the gate wants the bullet exact:
   ``frontmatter (`status: proposed`, `by: reader`, SQ8–SQ19 added to `inputs`)`` → ``frontmatter (`status: proposed`, SQ8–SQ19 added to `inputs`)``
######## P49
## Suggested fixes
The three earlier fixes (Context page, Self-definition, Interposition line counts) were applied at gate 3c and are no longer listed. Fixes below are for the follow-up-pass claims only; old text is exact text in `P49.md`.

1. *Reference* row (Extracted fields), Page column omits p.45, where the SQ17 range starts:
   `| 44, 46, 47, 50, 51 |` → `| 44, 45, 46, 47, 50, 51 |`

2. *Model mixing* (Extracted fields), the user-mode reason is stated for drivers only:
   `drivers and servers use "kernel calls" because in user mode they "cannot execute privileged instructions or read or write the computer's I/O ports"` → `the microkernel offers "kernel calls to authorized drivers and servers"; for drivers the stated reason is that they "run in user mode and cannot execute privileged instructions or read or write the computer's I/O ports"`
######## P66
## Suggested fixes
The earlier fixes (Context, J–Machine; Q3; Q6) were applied at gate 3c. The fixes below cover only the claims of the follow-up pass. Each one is in `P66.md`, in the *Notes* section.

1. **Criterion, SQ13 reason (differs).** In the *Criterion* bullet:
   - before: `SQ14 and SQ13: no scaling measured, two nodes only (p. 8);`
   - after: `SQ14: no scaling measured, two nodes only (p. 8); SQ13: the four clusters of a MAP share an on-chip cache (p. 2), so cores on a chip do not communicate only by messages, and the paper predates tapeout (p. 10), so it says nothing on adoption;`
2. **Criterion, SQ18 reason (differs).** In the *Criterion* bullet:
   - before: `SQ18: guarded-pointer costs are in [5], not here (p. 2–3);`
   - after: `SQ18: guarded pointers are described in [5] (p. 2–3), and this paper reports no cost for them;`

   - after: ``Changed: frontmatter (`status`, `inputs`);``
######## P70
## Suggested fixes

1. Reference, SQ15 (decentralised alternatives):
   `and the costs of decentralised alternatives, pp. 119–121)` → `with splitting the ID space proposed as the decentralised alternative at no stated cost, p. 120; costs are argued for parallel garbage collection and migration-based load management, pp. 120–121)`
2. Notes, Criteria bullet, SQ15 costs:
   `and decentralised GC and load management are argued to cost bandwidth, per-ID tracking or a full stop, pp. 119–121)` → `parallel GC is argued to cost per-ID tracking, a full stop or network bandwidth (p. 120), and migration-based load management to cost decision overhead and congestion at home nodes (p. 121), pp. 119–121)`
######## P102
## Suggested fixes

The three fixes proposed in the first check (Q6 row, Amdahl's law, message proxy page) were applied at gate 3c. The fixes below are for the follow-up claims only. Old text is exact text in `P102.md`.

1. **I4 page lists for SQ8 and SQ10 (differs):** the lists leave out pages that the record's own *What shapes programs* field (p. 6, 8) and *Model equivalence* field (p. 5) cite. The old string appears twice, in the *Reference* field and in the *Criterion* bullet of *Notes*. Replace both.
   - before: `SQ8 (p. 3, 4, 5, 7; argument only), SQ10 (p. 6, 8; argument only)`
   - after: `SQ8 (p. 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; argument only), SQ10 (p. 5, 6, 8; argument only)`

2. **Follow-up pass bullet, fields changed (differs):** `by` did not change in this pass.
   - before: ``Fields changed: frontmatter (`status`, `by`, `inputs`);``
   - after: ``Fields changed: frontmatter (`status`, `inputs`);``
######## P261
## Suggested fixes
The fixes from the first check (Reference page visibility, Q9, Levels with message semantics) were applied at gate 3c; the record now carries their wording. Fixes below are for the follow-up pass only.

1. Notes, follow-up bullet (SQ16), in `## Notes`:
   `the paper says bytecodes are "the semantic definition of the language" and the compiler has a Smalltalk version (p. 2)` → `the paper says "the virtual machine is the semantic definition of the language" and the compiler has a Smalltalk version (p. 2)`
######## P280
## Suggested fixes
The four earlier fixes were applied at gate 3c. The fixes below cover only the claims of the follow-up pass marked *differs*.

1. What shapes programs (correctness row), pp. 101–102:
   `HLLESF is a property of the whole system, whether implemented "mainly by hardware or mainly by software" (Attribute 8, p. 102), so the factor named is the cost of checking, not the hardware as such (inferred).`
   →
   `The paper presents HLLESF as an architectural measure, "an indication of how well the architecture supports a HLLCS" (p. 101), while Attribute 8 says that whether a HLLCS is implemented "mainly by hardware or mainly by software has no bearing on meeting the definition of a HLLCS" (p. 102). So the factor named is the execution cost of error checking on a given system, which the architecture affects but which hardware alone does not decide (inferred).`

2. Hardware–language trade-off (compiler optimisation row), p. 102:
   `Compilers will use traditional and advanced optimisations "provided that these advanced techniques do not impair the achievement of a HLLCS" (Attribute 9, p. 102).`
   →
   `Compilers "will use traditional code generation optimization techniques", and "very high performance machines may use advanced compiler techniques" such as common subexpression elimination, "provided that these advanced techniques do not impair the achievement of a HLLCS" (Attribute 9, p. 102).`

P. Deutsch", p. 68). **SQ18 met, narrowly.** It estimates the cost of object addressing itself (object-table indirection, 15% to 29%, analytical, p. 102), separately from the compiler. | Reference | Tanenbaum, Herder, Bos (2006), *Can We Make Operating Systems Reliable and Secure?*, IEEE Computer, May 2006, pp. 44–51; P49; I1 (I1(c), see Notes); I4 proposed (follow-up pass): SQ17 (pp. 45–47), SQ11 (p. 50). Publisher layout; printed page = PDF page + 43 | 44, 45, 46, 47, 50, 51 |
| Model mixing | Singularity (a message-passing OS; reported by P49's authors, who are not listed as its designers (inferred from the text and reference list, pp. 49–51)): a "shared object heap" is kept alongside channels; reason: "If all data, such as file blocks read from disk, had to go over channels, the system would be very slow, so an exception is made to the basic rule that each process's data is completely private and internal to itself" ("very slow" is asserted, not measured); the exception is bounded: "at each instant every object on the heap belongs to a single process. However, ownership of an object can be passed over a channel", giving data movement "from disk to user with zero copies". Its microkernel also "handles thread synchronization with mutexes" (no reason given). Minix 3 (stated by its designers (inferred: Herder is first author of the design paper [10], p. 51)): drivers and servers use "kernel calls" because in user mode they "cannot execute privileged instructions or read or write the computer's I/O ports"; "The clock driver shares the microkernel's address space" (no reason given). How often: not stated (one design per system; no population of programs is studied). These are system designs, not a study of application developers (inferred scope limit) | 47, 49, 50, 51 |
- **I4 proposed (follow-up pass): SQ17, SQ11.** SQ17: the paper describes two mechanisms that place a layer between drivers and a conventional kernel with few or no driver changes (Nooks wrappers on the virtual memory page map, pp. 45–46; drivers in paravirtualized Linux VMs on L4, pp. 46–47) and reports their coverage ("99 percent of the fatal driver errors and 55 percent of the nonfatal ones", plus named gaps, p. 46) and cost (455 hand-written wrappers, p. 46; 3,000 + 5,000 changed or added lines and "about 3 to 8 percent" overhead, p. 47), and that the Pentium "is not fully virtualizable" (p. 46); it does not compare these with interposition on messages. SQ11: one stated reason why a message-passing system keeps shared state (Singularity's shared heap, because channels alone "would be very slow", p. 50), reported third-party about Singularity and about an OS rather than application programs. I4 not met for SQ8: the bug-density and driver error-rate figures are cited from [1, 2, 3] (p. 44) and the paper attributes unreliability to kernel size and "very poor fault isolation" (p. 44), not to the hardware's execution model versus the language. I4 not met for SQ9: the Burroughs B5000 is mentioned as protection by "the Algol compiler's refusal to generate 'dangerous' code" (p. 49) with no argued cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface. SQ10, SQ12–SQ16, SQ18, SQ19: not answered (no duality argument, actor runtime, many-core, coordination-necessity, reflection, capability-hardware cost or post-Dennard adoption content); Singularity's trusted base (p. 49) is already in *Self-definition* under I1.
- **Follow-up pass (2026-10-13):** fields changed: *Reference* section (criteria sentence added); *Extracted fields* row *Reference* (I4 proposed added, pages 46, 47, 50 added); *Interposition* (coverage and paravirtualization concession appended for SQ17; earlier text unchanged); *Model mixing* (was `n/a (I1)`, now filled for SQ11); *Notes* (I4 bullet added; the earlier "Possible I4 relevance" bullet relabelled "Earlier flag, kept for the record", text otherwise unchanged); frontmatter (`status: proposed`, SQ1–SQ19 added to `inputs`). Source re-read: `papers/P49.pdf` (same publisher version, pp. 44–51).

However, ownership of an object can be passed over a channel", giving data movement "from disk to user with zero copies". Terms used: "IPC", "message passing", "messages".

- **X9 checked, not met:** the body reads partly as an overview ("we address four different approaches that researchers are using", p. 45), but the title and standfirst do not present it as a survey, and it reports its own measurements of Minix 3 (p. 49) and states a reason for microkernels' abandonment (p. 47).

- **Possible X8 overlap:** Minix 3's design is also in Herder et al., "Modular System Programming in MINIX 3", ;login: 2006 [10] (p. 51). If that paper or a later Minix 3 paper enters the review, X8 should be checked; I did not check the round file for it.

-- **I4 proposed (follow-up pass): SQ17, SQ11.** SQ17: the paper describes two mechanisms that place a layer between drivers and a conventional kernel with few or no driver changes (Nooks wrappers on the virtual memory page map, pp. 45–46; drivers in paravirtualized Linux VMs on L4, pp. 46–47) and reports their coverage ("99 percent of the fatal driver errors and 55 percent of the nonfatal ones", plus named gaps, p. 46) and cost (455 hand-written wrappers, p. 46; 3,000 + 5,000 changed or added lines and "about 3 to 8 percent" overhead, p. 47), and that the Pentium "is not fully virtualizable" (p. 46); it does not compare these with interposition on messages. SQ11: one stated reason why a message-passing system keeps shared state (Singularity's shared heap, because channels alone "would be very slow", p. 50), reported third-party about Singularity and about an OS rather than application programs.
